questions.q: Why do arrow functions matter inside an LWC component's class methods?
options: They don't create their own `this` binding, so `this` keeps referring to the component instance inside callbacks
They run faster than regular functions in every JavaScript engine
They are required by the `@api` decorator
They automatically make a property reactive
questions.explain: Arrow functions don't rebind `this`, which is exactly why they're used inside callbacks like `forEach` — `this` continues to refer to the surrounding component instance instead of the callback's own context.

questions.q: What does this destructuring statement do: `const { data, error } = result;`?
options: It creates a new object combining `data` and `error` into `result`
It deletes the `data` and `error` properties from `result`
It extracts the `data` and `error` properties from `result` into two separate local variables
It converts `result` into a template literal
questions.explain: Destructuring pulls named properties out of an object into standalone local variables in one step -- here, `data` and `error` come out of `result`.

questions.q: In `import { LightningElement, api, wire } from 'lwc';` followed by `import getContacts from '@salesforce/apex/ContactController.getContacts';`, why does the second import have no curly braces?
options: Because Apex imports never support named exports
Because curly braces are only required for class declarations
Because `getContacts` is the module's default export, while `LightningElement`, `api`, and `wire` are named exports pulled out with curly braces
There is no actual difference; both forms are interchangeable in LWC
questions.explain: A default import (no braces) pulls a module's single default export; named imports (in curly braces) pull out specific named exports. The imported Apex method is exposed as a default export, which is why it imports without braces.

questions.q: What problem does `async`/`await` solve when calling an Apex method imperatively?
options: It makes the Apex call run synchronously on the server
It converts the Apex method's return type from a Promise into a primitive value
It removes the need for a `try`/`catch` block entirely
It lets asynchronous, Promise-based code (like a server call) read top-to-bottom like synchronous code, instead of chaining `.then()`/`.catch()`
questions.explain: `async`/`await` is syntax for working with Promises that reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code, which is why it's commonly used for imperative Apex calls -- but errors still need to be caught, typically with `try`/`catch`.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend `const` and `let` over `var` in LWC code?
options: `var` is not supported at all by the LWC compiler
`var` can only hold numbers, not strings or objects
`const` and `let` are block-scoped, which avoids the subtle bugs caused by `var`'s looser scoping rules
Only `const` and `let` can be used inside a `@wire` adapter configuration
questions.explain: `const` and `let` use block scoping, which is more predictable than `var`'s function-level scoping -- that predictability is why modern JavaScript code, including virtually all LWC examples, avoids `var`.
